nodes.name: The ET-SoC-1 die

size.label: inferred
size.note: about 25.6-25.8 mm east-west by 22.1-22.2 mm north-south, scaled from Esperanto's die plot to 570 mm2 (chip.die-dims)

nodes.blurb: One slab of silicon about 26 by 22 mm, carrying over 24 billion transistors. It is a grid of 36 tiles called shires (32 compute shires, a master, a spare, a PCIe shire and an I/O shire), eight memory shires down the two sides, and an on-chip network joining them.

facts.text: Die area 570 mm².
facts.label: spec
facts.source: docs/findings/05-claims.md:513; docs/findings/01-resources.md:234 (R14: Hot Chips 33 slide 20; IEEE Micro 42(3) p.37)

facts.text: Die about 25.6-25.8 mm east-west by 22.1-22.2 mm north-south (width/height 1.15-1.17), from the published die plot scaled to 570 mm²; the shire grid spans about 86% of the die's width, the rest being the memory shires and their DRAM PHYs down each side (about 1.76 mm per side).
facts.label: inferred
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/geometry/pitch.json, `scale_from_570mm2.A_black_layout_region` and `.B_symmetric_bottom` (`die_w_mm`, `die_h_mm`, `grid_w_mm`, `memshire_col_w_mm`); heat-per-mm page §'How long is a hop'

facts.text: TSMC 7 nm, over 24 billion transistors, 89 mask layers (Esperanto, Hot Chips 33 and IEEE Micro 2022).
facts.label: spec
facts.source: docs/findings/05-claims.md:513; docs/findings/01-resources.md:91-104 (R6)

facts.text: Average density: 24 billion transistors over 570 mm2 is about 42 million per mm2, less than half the ~91 MTr/mm2 of TSMC N7's dense logic cells; SRAM periphery, analog blocks (PLLs, PHYs), I/O and wiring take the rest.
facts.label: derived
facts.source: arithmetic on chip.process and chip.die-area; the N7 figure: Wikipedia, "7 nm process", comparison table, row TSMC N7 (gate pitch 57 nm, fin pitch 30 nm, minimum metal pitch 40 nm, 91.2-96.5 MTr/mm2, SRAM cell 0.027 um2; fins SAQP, gates and M0-M4 SADP), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7_nm_process (read 30 Sep 2026)

facts.text: Package is 45.0 × 45.0 mm (lid 44.8) with 2,494 balls and over 30,000 bumps to the die; the package drawing shows no die outline.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/SYNTHESIS.md §1a row 'Package' (citing external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf p.33 Fig. 9-1 and HC33 slide 20)

facts.text: The ET-SoC-1 has 1,093 RISC-V cores: 1,088 ET-Minions, 4 ET-Maxions and 1 Minion-based service processor.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.4 (§1 Product Overview); external/et-man/ET Programmer's Reference Manual.pdf, pdf p.7 (§1)

nodes.name: Compute shire

size.label: inferred
size.note: one tile pitch: 3.73 mm east-west, 3.70 north-south, measured in pixels on the die plot (chip.hop-pitch)

nodes.blurb: A tile of 32 small cores (minions) in four neighbourhoods, with 4 MB of shared on-chip memory, a crossbar joining them, and one stop on the on-chip network. All 34 minion shires are the same design; 32 of them run the programs.

facts.text: A minion shire is 4 neighbourhoods = 32 minions = 64 harts, a four-bank 4 MB shared L2/L3/scratchpad cache, a mesh stop, a crossbar between them, and an uncacheable (UC) block with fast local barriers, fast credit counters, inter-processor interrupts and global atomics.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.5 (§2.1); external/et-man/ET Minion Overview.pdf, pdf p.4 (slide 5)

facts.text: A minion-shire cell is about 13.8–13.95 mm²; the 34 minion shires take about 468–474 mm² (82–83% of the die).
facts.label: derived
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/SYNTHESIS.md §1a row 'Minion-shire cell area'

facts.text: Shire top level: the main NoC interface (ports to_l3 ×4, to_sys, l3_slave ×4, uc_to_l3, uc_to_sys, sys_slave) sits above the shire channel (shire cache with 4 banks, UC block, RBOX, ESR, I$ memories), which feeds the four neighbourhoods; clock domains CLOCK_NOC, SHIRE_CLOCK, NEIGH_CLOCK, with the PLL/DLL, sensors and debug NoC bridge below.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET Minion Shire Description.pdf p.5 Figure 1

facts.text: A shire spans several voltage domains separated by level shifters and FIFOs: minions on the low-voltage minion rail, the SRAM arrays (shire cache, and the I-cache data memory, placed in the shire channel because it must run at high voltage) on the SRAM rail, the mesh stop on the NoC rail.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET Minion Shire Description.pdf, pdf p.4, p.10 (§3.1) and p.18 (§5); docs/research/why-low-power.md:23-28 (R6)

facts.text: Each minion shire has its own PLL; the shire cache and minions run on the shire clock (the neighbourhood clock is the same clock shifted 180°), outside the NoC's clock domain. Design value 1,000 MHz.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET Minion Shire Description.pdf, pdf p.4 and pdf p.12 (Table 2: o_clkpll_shire, o_clkpll_neigh)

facts.text: Per-shire on-die voltage at idle (34 minion shires): minion rail 517–521 mV, lows 513 (shires 0, 1, 2, 18) to 520, highs to 522; SRAM 703–707 mV; mesh 483–486 mV.
facts.label: measured
facts.source: docs/findings/05-claims.md:41 (docs/reports/data/2026-09-20-power-aifoundry2/per-shire-voltage-idle.json)

selectable.tooltip: Shire N, compute shire. Space for details; Enter zooms in.

nodes.name: Mesh stop

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude only: nine 512-bit routers and their crossings; no floorplan of the shire is published (L114, l2.floorplan)

nodes.blurb: Where the shire joins the on-chip network. Every request that leaves the shire, and every one that comes in, passes through its routers, which pass packets on to the four neighbouring stops.

facts.text: Each shire meets the mesh at a single point: minion 31 of each shire gives the same round trips as minion 0.
facts.label: measured
facts.source: on-chip communication page §'What the numbers say'

facts.text: Each mesh stop has 9 main-NoC routers (layers 0–8) plus one debug-NoC router; routers have 8 ports (H, E, S, W, N, I, J, K) with 4 VC slots each; route info, packet, sideband and data are parity-protected (no ECC).
facts.label: spec
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/SYNTHESIS.md §1b rows 'Main-NoC layers', 'Router ports and VCs', 'Error protection' (etsoc_shire_other_esr.h:3877-3981; noc_esr.h)

facts.text: A shire has 4 to_l3 master and 4 L3 slave lanes to the mesh; the lane is chosen by PA[7:6], so lines i and i+4 share a lane (a 1 KB load puts 4 of its 16 lines on each).
facts.label: spec
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/report.json inputs.lanes (core-et-main shirecache_mesh_master.sv:141-153); docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/SYNTHESIS.md §1b 'Lanes'

facts.text: Every shire's NoC port is 512 bits wide: one 64 B line per beat, single-beat only.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/report.json inputs.port_bits (core-et rtl/inc/axi_defines.vh:43 SC_MESH_MASTER_AXI_DATA_SIZE 512)

facts.text: The mesh (routers, links, NetSpeed bridges) is on its own low-voltage rail at 0.485 V (0.484 V at the die).
facts.label: measured
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/report.json inputs.noc_v (telemetry reg_mv.noc 485 / die_mv.noc 484); docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/SYNTHESIS.md §1b 'Voltage domain'

facts.text: The NoC runs at 400 MHz on these cards (every telemetry sample). The design's NoC clock is 500 MHz (from PLL2 in the I/O shire), and the firmware's DVFS table allows 300-500 MHz.
facts.label: measured
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-20-power-aifoundry2/horace-telemetry.jsonl (and horace2-, thermal-telemetry.jsonl: 3,681 samples, 20 Sep), field `mhz.noc`; external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET Minion Shire Description.pdf, pdf p.12 (Table 2, clk__noc); external/et-platform/device-bootloaders/src/ServiceProcessorBL2/services/thermal_pwr_mgmt.c:134-135

nodes.name: Router (one of nine main-NoC layers)

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude: an 8-port router with 512-bit datapaths; the NetSpeed configuration is not in the repository

nodes.blurb: A small switch. Packets arrive on its input ports, wait in short queues, and an arbiter decides which one crosses the router's internal switch to which output each cycle. Each mesh stop has nine of them stacked as separate networks, plus one for debug.

facts.text: Each mesh stop has 9 main-NoC routers (layers 0–8) plus one debug-NoC router; routers have 8 ports (H, E, S, W, N, I, J, K) with 4 VC slots each; route info, packet, sideband and data are parity-protected (no ECC).
facts.label: spec
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/SYNTHESIS.md §1b rows 'Main-NoC layers', 'Router ports and VCs', 'Error protection' (etsoc_shire_other_esr.h:3877-3981; noc_esr.h)

facts.text: GENERIC. A mesh router stage: input virtual-channel buffers (flip-flop or register-file arrays), route computation, virtual-channel and switch allocators (arbiters), a crossbar of multiplexers, and output drivers onto the link; each link is a bundle of wires broken by repeaters (inverter pairs) every few hundred microns.
facts.label: generic
facts.source: textbook (Dally and Towles, Principles and Practices of Interconnection Networks)

facts.text: UNKNOWN. The router pipeline per hop (4 NoC cycles each way is derived), which of the 9 main-NoC layers carries L3 requests and replies, and the flit width. The dimension order, asked here until 29 September, is measured (l3.route).
facts.label: unknown
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/SYNTHESIS.md:66-68, 75-76; the order: docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-nocr (E56)

facts.text: 20 ns per hop round trip is 10 ns, or 4 cycles of the 400 MHz NoC clock, per hop each way, if request and reply take equal time.
facts.label: derived
facts.source: l3.hop with l3.clock; docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/SYNTHESIS.md:76

facts.text: At least 117 B cross one link direction per 400 MHz NoC cycle (at least 936 data bits), more than one 512-bit layer carries: the link was not saturated in that test.
facts.label: measured
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/SYNTHESIS.md §1b row 'Measured data per link direction' (docs/reports/data/2026-09-23-energy-manual/catalogue.json wire/hop1)

nodes.name: Input buffers (virtual channels)

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude: 8 ports x 4 VC slots of a flit (512 bits or more) each, if flip-flops

nodes.blurb: Short queues at each input where packets wait their turn. Each port has four slots (virtual channels), so one blocked packet does not stop the others.

facts.text: Routers have 8 ports (H, E, S, W, N, I, J, K) with 4 VC slots each.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/SYNTHESIS.md §1b rows 'Main-NoC layers', 'Router ports and VCs', 'Error protection' (etsoc_shire_other_esr.h:3877-3981; noc_esr.h)

facts.text: If every slot holds one 512-bit flit, one router buffers 8 x 4 x 512 = 16,384 bits, about 147,000 bits over the nine layers of one stop.
facts.label: inferred
facts.source: arithmetic on L105 with an estimated flit width (SYNTHESIS.md row "Flit width", unknown): inferred, the weakest of its inputs

facts.text: Router input buffers are flip-flop or register-file arrays (textbook).
facts.label: generic
facts.source: textbook (Dally and Towles, Principles and Practices of Interconnection Networks)

nodes.name: Route computation and allocators

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude: arbitration logic for 8 ports

nodes.blurb: Logic that reads each packet's destination, picks the output (x first, then y, for a request), and arbitrates when two packets want the same output in the same cycle.

facts.text: The mesh routes in dimension order, and a request and its reply take opposite orders: a request goes x first, then y, and a reply y first, then x, on the logical map, so a reply retraces its request's route backwards. Measured on 29 September (E56) with sets of streams between shires chosen so that their streams share one directed link under one order and none under the other: 1 KB tensor loads, whose data travel as replies, fell to 0.54-0.77 of their bandwidth alone when they shared a link under y first and held at 1.00 when they shared one under x first; tensor stores, whose data travel as requests, showed the mirror (0.52-0.76 against 1.00). A shared link carried about 92 GB/s. The same on aifoundry1 card 1 (development), aifoundry3 (the frozen validation) and aifoundry2 (the same frozen test, run as a third card on the evening of 29 September), three passes each.
facts.label: measured
facts.source: tools/claims-v3/nocr/PREREG.md (frozen 29 Sep about 00:10 PDT, sha256 2472ab3e...; the sets: workloads/nocroute/meshmap.py, tools/claims-v3/nocr/sets.json); docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-nocr/raw/<card>/summary.json .r32.read and .r32.write: .verdict, .sets.<set>.rho_pooled (sets of 3 and 5 streams), .capacity_gbs_from_dropping_sets; docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-nocr/README.md

facts.text: Route computation, a virtual-channel allocator and a switch allocator (arbiters) pick which packet crosses the switch each cycle (textbook).
facts.label: generic
facts.source: textbook (Dally and Towles, Principles and Practices of Interconnection Networks)

nodes.name: Router switch (crossbar)

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude: an 8 x 8 switch of 512-bit or wider datapaths

nodes.blurb: A grid of multiplexers that connects any input port to any output port for one cycle. It is wide: a whole 64-byte cache line moves in one beat.

facts.text: Every shire's NoC port is 512 bits wide: one 64 B line per beat, single-beat only.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/report.json inputs.port_bits (core-et rtl/inc/axi_defines.vh:43 SC_MESH_MASTER_AXI_DATA_SIZE 512)

facts.text: A crossbar of multiplexers joins the inputs to the output drivers (textbook).
facts.label: generic
facts.source: textbook (Dally and Towles, Principles and Practices of Interconnection Networks)

nodes.name: Voltage and clock crossing (VCFIFO)

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude: a FIFO of a few 512-bit entries with level shifters on every bit

nodes.blurb: The shire's cache runs at 0.705 V on its own clock, the network at 0.485 V and 400 MHz. Every bit that crosses is shifted in voltage and re-timed through two flip-flops into the other clock, so it cannot be caught half-changed.

facts.text: The neighbourhood's per-bank output FIFOs double as the clock- and voltage-crossing elements: semi-synchronous VC FIFOs from the cell library, with level shifters built in at the HV/LV boundary. Their storage cells always sit in the HV region 'as performance and access time improve with the voltage'. Responses cross back through a VC FIFO at the neighbourhood's input.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Neigborhood-MAS.pdf, pdf p.18-19 §4.3.4, pdf p.20 §4.4.1, pdf p.45 §7.1 (Figure 16)

facts.text: The Shire Channel, which holds the shire cache, the UC block and the I-cache data memory, is a high-voltage region: the I-cache memory sits there 'because it has to be operated at high voltage'. The mesh routers sit on their own low-voltage rail, and the router side of each crossing is low voltage.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET Minion Shire Description.pdf pdf p.10 §3.1 and pdf p.18 §5; external/core-et/rtl/libs/mems_and_fifos/vcfifo_nsip_brdg2rtr.v:9 (via docs/reports/data/2026-09-24-wire-energy/research/SYNTHESIS.md:74)

facts.text: GENERIC. A voltage and clock crossing: a level shifter (cross-coupled PMOS over an NMOS differential input pair) lifts or drops the signal swing, and a 2-flip-flop synchroniser (as the spec's VCFIFO uses) samples it in the receiving clock, costing 2-3 receiving-clock cycles.
facts.label: generic
facts.source: textbook; the 2 stages are et-spec (external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.11)

facts.text: The ET cell library has level shifters in both directions (vclevel_shft_h2l, vclevel_shft_l2h) and VCFIFO memories and synchronisers (vcfifo_mem, vcfifo_wr_hiv_*, vcfifo_wr_lov_*, et_cdc_sync) for these crossings.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/rtl/libs/mems_and_fifos/ (file names)

facts.text: Another shire's scratchpad: 99.84 + 12.00 cycles per mesh hop at 600 MHz (112-220 cycles, 186-366 ns over 1-10 hops); all 124 points within one cycle; a to b equals b to a within 0.032 cycles, on three cards.
facts.label: measured
facts.source: docs/findings/05-claims.md:423; lat.json items[LAT-M3].per_card.<card>.passes[] (row0_slope 11.998-12.002, frac_within_1 1.0)

reuse.how: the crossing scale draws a VC FIFO cell with a level shifter (cross-coupled PMOS over an NMOS pair); the same drawing serves the mesh stop's 0.705 V to 0.485 V crossing with the rails relabelled

nodes.name: Shire cache (four banks)

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude: 4 MB of SRAM macros (about 1.1 mm2 of bitcells if HD 6T, more with periphery) and their logic

nodes.blurb: The shire's shared 4 MB of fast on-chip memory, in four banks. One memory, three uses: part of it is the shire's cache (L2), part a slice of the chip-wide cache (L3), and part a scratchpad programs manage themselves.

facts.text: The shire cache is 4 MB: 4 banks × 1 MB, each bank 4 sub-banks; L2 and L3 are 4-way set-associative, 64-byte lines, write-back and write-allocate, with SECDED ECC on tags, data and state.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf, pdf p.8-9 (§1.1: 'The POR for the first SoC is 4M/Shire, 4 banks/Shire, 4 sub-banks/bank'); external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.13 (§2.1.3.1)

facts.text: Mode M0, the reset mode and the one these cards run: per shire 2.5 MB scratchpad, 512 KB L2, 1 MB L3 slice; over 32 shires 80 MB scratchpad, 16 MB L2, 32 MB L3.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf, pdf p.21-22 (Tables 6-7, 'The chip will come out of reset in mode M0'); external/core-et/rtl/shire/esr/esr_cache_bank.v:106 ('default cache config mode = M0'); external/et-man/ET Minion Overview.pdf, pdf p.4

facts.text: The L3 is not a separate memory. It is the top quarter of the same arrays that hold the L2 and the scratchpad: in each data macro (4,096 words) the L3 lines are words 3,072-4,095 (address {set 768-1023, way}); in each tag and tag-state macro (1,024 rows) rows 768-1023. Per shire that is a quarter of 64 data, 16 tag and 16 tag-state macros.
facts.label: derived
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.22 Table 7 (L3 base 0x300, end 0x3FF), pdf p.51 (macro sizes); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe_sub_bank.sv:1613 (data RAM address = {pipe_set, tag_ram_hit_way}); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe.sv:1010 (one tag, tag-state and data RAM wrapper per sub-bank); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe_data_ram_wrap.sv:83-107 (four quadword RAMs)

facts.text: Per shire there are 64 data macros (4 banks x 4 sub-banks x 4 panels), 16 tag macros and 16 tag-state macros.
facts.label: derived
facts.source: derived from external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.48 §2.14.5, p.47 §2.14.2-3 and p.51

facts.text: Bits stored per shire, ECC included: data 64 x 4,096 x 144 = 37,748,736; tag 16 x 1,024 x 116 = 1,900,544; tag state 16 x 1,024 x 40 = 655,360; 40,304,640 in all (about 40.3 Mbit, of which 33.6 Mbit is the 4 MB of data).
facts.label: derived
facts.source: derived from the macro sizes, external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.51

facts.text: If the single-port data and tag macros use a 6-transistor cell and the two-port tag-state file an 8-transistor cell (the usual choice for such macros), one shire's cache arrays hold about 243 million cell transistors (39.6 Mbit x 6 + 0.66 Mbit x 8), before any periphery.
facts.label: generic
facts.source: l2.bits x GENERIC 6T/8T bitcells

facts.text: At TSMC N7's 0.027 um2 high-density 6T cell, the shire cache's 40.3 Mbit of cells would take about 1.1 mm2, about 8% of the 13.9 mm2 shire tile, before the macros' periphery; which bitcell the macros use is not documented.
facts.label: inferred
facts.source: arithmetic on l2.bits and S.-Y. Wu et al. (TSMC), "A 7nm CMOS platform technology featuring 4th generation FinFET transistors with a 0.027um2 high density 6-T SRAM cell for mobile SoC applications", IEDM 2016, paper 2.6; the bitcell is asked (u.bitcell)

facts.text: "These SRAM banks operate near the process-nominal supply voltage to allow higher density than the smaller caches within each core."
facts.label: spec
facts.source: D. Ditzel et al., "Accelerating ML Recommendation With Over 1,000 RISC-V/Tensor Processors on Esperanto's ET-SoC-1 Chip", IEEE Micro 42(3), May/June 2022 (https://www.esperanto.ai/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Dave-IEEE-Micro.pdf), p. 35

nodes.name: Bank (one of four)

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude: a quarter of the shire cache

nodes.blurb: Each bank is a complete cache of its own, with a queue of waiting requests, a pipeline and four sub-banks of memory. Consecutive 64-byte lines go to banks 0, 1, 2, 3 in turn, so the four work in parallel.

facts.text: The shire cache is four identical banks; each bank is an independent L2 cache with its own request queue, pipeline and next-level ports. A bank takes at most one request per cycle and returns at most one 512-bit line per cycle.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.6 §1; pdf p.30 §2.1

facts.text: L2 and scratchpad requests go to the bank chosen by PA[7:6], so consecutive 64 B lines rotate through banks 0-3.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.6 §1 and p.24 §1.4.1.1

facts.text: Per bank: a 64-entry request queue (up to 21 entries reserved for L3-slave requests), an 8-entry read buffer and a 32-entry write-around coalescing buffer; L3-slave requests take priority over local L2 requests.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: docs/research/counters-and-dram.md:458-465; external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf, pdf p.9 (coalescing buffer, 32 entries per bank) and pdf p.36 (arbitration)

facts.text: With 2-cycle RAMs a sub-bank accepts a new request only every other cycle (3-cycle RAMs: every third). Operations that need two RAM passes (a fill that may evict, an atomic) reserve bubble slots, because the pipeline never stalls once a request is scheduled.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.35-36 §2.6, pdf p.35 §2.5

facts.text: Load-to-use latency by pointer chase at 600 MHz: read-buffer hit 36.00 cycles (60 ns) and L2 or own-scratchpad hit 47.00 cycles (78 ns) on hart 0; hart 1 pays 3 more (39.0 and 50.0). Every pass on every card fell within 35.998-36.006 and 46.998-47.024.
facts.label: measured
facts.source: docs/findings/05-claims.md:421; docs/reports/data/2026-09-25-claims-v3/results/lat.json items[LAT-M1].per_card.<card>.passes[] (RB, L2, hart1)

facts.text: With 1 KB tensor loads on every minion the L2 delivers 2.45 TB/s chip-wide: 4.0 B per minion-cycle = 128 B per shire-cycle, half the four banks' 256 B per shire-cycle. The own scratchpad gives the same (2.46 TB/s).
facts.label: measured
facts.source: docs/findings/05-claims.md:380, 546; docs/findings/15-earlier-findings.md:98

nodes.name: Request queue

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude: 64 entries of address and state

nodes.blurb: A list of the requests the bank is working on, like a to-do list: 64 entries, each kept from its arrival until its data is back, so many misses can be outstanding at once.

facts.text: Each bank has a 64-entry request queue (reqq), the equivalent of MSHRs. An entry lives from allocation through miss, mesh read, fill and any victim write-back. Two entries can be allocated per cycle (one neighbourhood, one L3-slave request), and 21 of the 64 are reserved for L3-slave requests by default.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.34-35 §2.5-2.6; external/core-et/rtl/inc/shire_cache_defines.vh:69; external/core-et/rtl/shire/esr/esr_cache_bank.v:81 (NUM_REQQ_ENTRIES/3)

facts.text: Choosing what enters the pipeline takes three steps: round-robin per sub-bank (neighbourhood and L3 separately), then L3 requests before neighbourhood requests, then masking out busy sub-banks and a round-robin across sub-banks. Errata RTLMIN-6207 and 6214 record that a neighbourhood request can starve behind L3-slave traffic.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.36 §2.6 Figure 8; external/et-man/ET-SoC Errata.pdf, pdf p.80-81 §4.1-4.2

nodes.name: Read buffer

size.label: inferred
size.note: 8 x 512 bits = 4,096 flip-flops at about 1 um2 each (an N7 flip-flop, inference) is about 0.004 mm2, 65 um on a side

nodes.blurb: Eight recently read lines kept in registers next to the pipeline. A repeat read is served from here without waking the big memory panels: 36 cycles instead of 47.

facts.text: Read buffer (RBUF): an 8-entry fully associative mini-cache of clean lines per bank (2 KB per shire). Lines are installed on L2 and scratchpad read hits. Requests are checked against it when they are allocated a reqq entry, and hits are served from it without touching the RAM panels, 'as these memory panels are slow and power hungry'. Anything that will change the data RAM clears the entry, and a 4-entry FIFO holds hit responses.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.9 §1.1, pdf p.40 §2.8; external/core-et/rtl/inc/shire_cache_defines.vh:273-275

facts.text: The RBUF is on by default (esr_sc_l2_rbuf_enable = esr_sc_scp_rbuf_enable = 1 in the RTL's ESR init), and the cards show it: a 36-cycle plateau for working sets of 768 B to 2 KB, then 47 cycles from 4 KB, on all three cards.
facts.label: derived
facts.source: external/core-et/rtl/shire/esr/esr_cache_bank.v:311-312; docs/reports/data/2026-09-25-claims-v3/results/lat.json items[LAT-M1] (knees between 512/768 B and 2/4 KB)

facts.text: What the RBUF is built from on silicon is not documented. The Ainekko reimplementation keeps it as 8 x 512-bit registers (flip-flops) holding ECC-corrected data, with an LRU replacement arbiter and a 7-stage pending-install pipeline.
facts.label: unknown
facts.source: external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe_rbuf.sv:1-20, 105, 416-419

nodes.name: Data queue

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude: 64 lines of 576 bits in a two-port register file

nodes.blurb: A holding area for the data of requests in flight: one 64-byte line per request-queue entry.

facts.text: The dataq holds one 64 B line per reqq entry in a two-ported register file (one write and one read port, each shared by 5 sources). BIST sees it as logical RAM mbq (64 x 4 x 144 bits, 1-cycle access) plus mbb (64 x 72 bits). Read hits normally bypass it straight to the response mux.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.35, pdf p.38-40 §2.7, pdf p.49; external/core-et/rtl/inc/shire_cache_defines.vh:350-380

facts.text: Each bank has a 32-entry coalescing buffer that merges write-arounds (TensorStores to L3 or a remote scratchpad) in the L2. It flushes a line once all four 128-bit quadwords are written, or on an explicit flush.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.9 §1.1, pdf p.42 §2.10; external/core-et/rtl/inc/shire_cache_defines.vh:282

nodes.name: Atomic unit

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude: a 256-bit ALU

nodes.blurb: A small arithmetic unit beside the memory that performs read-modify-write operations (add, swap, min, max ...) on a word in one place, so that many cores can update a shared counter without racing.

facts.text: Each bank has an atomic unit (32-, 64- and 256-bit operands: swap, add, and, or, xor, min/max signed and unsigned, float min/max). An atomic keeps its sub-bank busy from the read through the operation to the write.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.36 item 3, pdf p.40-41 §2.9

facts.text: A global atomic on a scratchpad word is performed by the home bank's atomic block (read, ALU, write; the sub-bank is held busy throughout) after arriving on the L3-slave port; the bank retires one every 10.00 cycles; an uncontended remote atomic takes 216 cycles round trip; an atomic through the self ID 0x7F is a bus error.
facts.label: measured
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf p.17 (L3 slave REQ_Atomic, local SCP), p.36, p.40 §2.9; docs/findings/05-claims.md:232; docs/findings/17-hot-line.md:35-38; lat.json [item=LAT-H]

nodes.name: Bank pipeline

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude: the stage registers and control of one bank

nodes.blurb: The assembly line a request moves through, one stage per clock: allocate, arbitrate, read the tags, check them, compare, read the data, check it, send it. Registers between the stages hold each request's state.

facts.text: Read-hit pipeline stages (2-cycle RAMs): ag (reqq allocate), ad (dependencies), rqa (reqq arbitration), tap, ta, ta0, ta1 (tag and tag-state RAM access), te (tag ECC), tc (tag compare: hit, victim), dap, da, da0, da1 (data RAM access), de (data ECC), dc (data complete: OR'd across the sub-banks, then to the response mux, or the dataq if the mux is busy).
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.44 figure, pdf p.45-46 §2.14.1

facts.text: If each named stage is one cycle, the 15 stages from reqq allocation to data complete account for 15 of the spec's 21-cycle L2 hit, leaving about 6 cycles for the request crossbar, response mux and response crossbar. The spec cites an 'L2 and L3 Pipeline stages Spreadsheet' that has the real budget, which we do not have.
facts.label: derived
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.11 Table 1, pdf p.44-46, pdf p.131 ref. 3

facts.text: Module-level clock gaters (esr_sc_clk_gate_disable) stop the bank's clock when it has no outstanding requests (errata RTLMIN-6235, which is why the bank's cycle counter under-counts). The reimplementation gates each RAM's clock on only for the ram_delay cycles of an access.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.97 §4.1; external/et-man/ET-SoC Errata.pdf, pdf p.82 §4.3; external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe_data_ram_wrap.sv:1-7, 46-66

facts.text: Each bank has a performance monitor: a cycle counter and two 40-bit event counters, which can count RBUF hits, tag hits and misses, victims and opcodes. They are M-mode registers. A U-mode kernel can only read them (syscall 9) with the firmware's default qualifier, which counts all read-type requests and does not separate hits from misses.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.104-109 §4.9; docs/research/counters-and-dram.md:186-191, 252, 259

nodes.name: Sub-bank

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude: four data panels of about 150 um plus a tag and a state macro

nodes.blurb: A quarter of a bank: its own tag memory (which lines are here), state memory (valid, dirty, LRU), and four data panels that together hold one 64-byte line per row.

facts.text: Each bank is four sub-banks. Each sub-bank has its own tag RAM, tag-state RAM, data RAM and ECC logic; the read buffer, atomic unit and coalescing buffer are shared by the bank's four sub-banks.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.35 §2.5; pdf p.9 ('4 sub-banks/bank' is the POR for the first SoC)

facts.text: A sub-bank holds 4,096 lines = 1,024 sets x 4 ways (4 MB / 64 B / 4 banks / 4 sub-banks).
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.20 Table 4

facts.text: The lookup is serial (tag first, then data): the data-RAM address includes the way, and the data stages (dap..dc) start after the tag compare (tc), so a hit reads only the hit way's row, not all four ways.
facts.label: derived
facts.source: external/core-et/rtl/inc/shire_cache_defines.vh:253 (SC_DATA_RAM_ADDR_SIZE = way + set); external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.44 read-hit stage figure

facts.text: Only the panels holding the addressed quadwords are enabled (a 3-quadword partial write activates 3 panels), and the RAM inputs, address bits included, are held unchanged in cycles with no access, to save power.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.48 §2.14.5; pdf p.46 §2.14.1.5 and §2.14.1.11

size.label: inferred
size.note: 118,784 bits at 0.027 um2 is 0.0032 mm2 (57 um square) of cells, more with periphery; if HD 6T (inference)

nodes.blurb: A small memory that stores, for every set, which four lines (tags) are in it, so a lookup can tell hit from miss.

facts.text: Tag RAM: one row per set holding all four ways' tags, each 23 bits + 6 ECC bits, so the row is 116 bits and the four tags are read and compared in parallel.

facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.47 §2.14.2; external/core-et/rtl/inc/shire_cache_defines.vh:241-246

nodes.name: Tag-state RAM (1,024 x 40, two-port)

size.label: inferred
size.note: 40,960 bits; a two-port cell is larger than a 6T cell (order of magnitude)

nodes.blurb: A memory read and written on every request: which lines are valid, dirty, locked or all zeros, and the order in which they were used. It has two ports so the read and the update happen in one pass.

facts.text: Tag-state RAM: one 40-bit row per set = 4 x {valid, locked, zero, qwen[3:0]} + 5-bit LRU code + 7-bit ECC. It is read and written on every L2 request, and it is two-ported, so the read and the LRU/dirty update happen in the same pass.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.47 §2.14.3 Table 12 and pdf p.45; external/core-et/rtl/inc/shire_cache_defines.vh:231-237

facts.text: The tag-state RAM is 'saculs0g4l2p1024x40m4b1w0c0p0d0s1rm0rw11', RAM type 2PUHDRF: 1,024 words x 40 bits. The spec says the state RAM is two-ported (a read and a write per request).

facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.51 §2.14.6.4, pdf p.45

facts.text: Zero lines skip the data array. When a fill or a full-line write brings an all-zero line (the bank computes the NOR of all 512 bits as the line arrives), the tag state's zero bit is set and the data macros are not written; a later read of that line does not read them either and returns zeros. Enabled by default (esr_sc_zero_state_enable = 1).
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf pdf p.47 Table 12 ('zero ... cache memory must not be read') and pdf p.101 (esr_sc_zero_state_enable); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_bank_mesh.sv:346 (zero_data = ~|data); external/core-et-main/hw/ip/shirecache/rtl/shirecache_pipe_sub_bank.sv:810 (no data RAM read on a zero hit), 983-1001, 1051-1063 (no data RAM write)

nodes.name: Data panel (4,096 x 144 SRAM macro)

size.label: inferred
size.note: 589,824 bits x 0.027 um2 = 0.016 mm2 of cells; if the array is 1,024 rows x 576 columns of 114 x 237 nm cells it is about 117 x 137 um, some 150 um with its periphery (inference on the unconfirmed m4 reading and the HD cell)

nodes.blurb: The basic memory block: a compiled SRAM macro holding 4,096 words of 144 bits (128 data bits and 16 error-check bits). A shire has 64 of them; a line is one row across four panels. Inside: a grid of storage cells, with decoders down one side and sense amplifiers along the bottom.

facts.text: The data panel is the compiled macro 'saduls0g4l1p4096x144m4b4w0c0p0d0s1rm0sdrw11', RAM type 1PUHD: 4,096 words x 144 bits.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.51 §2.14.6.4

facts.text: Data RAM: each sub-bank is four 144-bit-wide panels, each holding one 128-bit quadword + 16 ECC bits (8 per 64 bits). A 64 B line is one row across the four panels (576 bits); a sub-bank's data RAM is 4,096 rows addressed by {way, set}.

facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.48 §2.14.5 and pdf p.48-49 §2.14.6.2; external/core-et/rtl/inc/shire_cache_defines.vh:250-255

facts.text: The tag-state, tag and data panels are 'IP acquired from a third party vendor'. They are tested with a shared-bus BIST 'such as the Synopsys SMS (STAR Memory System)'. The BIST's logical RAMs per bank are mbs (tag state), mbt (tag), mbd (data), mbq (dataq) and mbi (instruction cache, bank 0 only).

facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Shire-Cache-Specification.pdf (v1.1), pdf p.48 §2.14.6.1 and pdf p.49 §2.14.6.3

facts.text: The macros' vendor is not named. Three hints point to Synopsys-compiled memories: Ainekko's translation guide lists 'Synopsys ASIC SRAMs (saduls0g4l1p*, etc.)', the spec's BIST is 'a shared bus BIST, such as the Synopsys SMS', and the BIST wrappers in the open build script are named sms_sram_wr_<macro>. size.label: inferred
size.note: a strip the height of the array (inference)

nodes.blurb: Turns the row number into one active wordline: small logic gates decode the address, and a strong driver per row raises that row's wordline across all 576 columns.

facts.label: generic
facts.source: textbook

facts.text: GENERIC. Read-margin trims adjust the self-timed sense-enable delay (often from a replica bitline); read assist lowers the wordline voltage to protect the cell from read upset. These are standard knobs of FinFET-era SRAM compilers.
facts.label: generic
facts.source: GENERIC (textbook single-port 6T SRAM; not from an ET source)

nodes.name: Precharge, column mux, sense amplifiers, write drivers

size.label: inferred
size.note: a strip the width of the array (inference)

nodes.blurb: The circuits along the bottom edge. Before a read they charge every bitline pair high; a tiny difference then appears on the selected pair, and a sense amplifier turns it into a full 0 or 1. For a write, drivers force the bitlines.

facts.text: GENERIC. In a differential read exactly one bitline of each pair discharges whether the cell holds 0 or 1, so the array's read energy is to first order independent of the data; data dependence comes from what follows the sense amplifiers (outputs that toggle, buses, ECC) unless the macro uses a precharged single-ended global read line.
facts.label: generic
facts.source: GENERIC (textbook single-port 6T SRAM; not from an ET source)

facts.text: GENERIC. A write: write drivers pull one bitline of each selected pair to ground, the wordline rises, and the access transistor overpowers the cell's PMOS pull-up so the cell flips. Write assist (for example a negative bitline or a lowered cell supply) and a longer write pulse make the flip reliable at low voltage.
facts.label: generic
facts.source: textbook

facts.text: GENERIC. Read assist usually lowers the wordline voltage so a read cannot flip a weak cell; read-margin settings delay the sense-amplifier enable so more bitline swing develops, slower but safer at low voltage.
facts.label: generic
facts.source: textbook; memory-compiler datasheets

size.label: inferred

nodes.blurb: A clock gate that lets the panel's clock run only for the cycles it is accessed, and the self-timing that decides when the sense amplifiers fire (the trims set its margins).

size.label: inferred
size.note: if 8 minions of about 0.25 mm2 plus the neighbourhood's logic make about 2.4 mm2, about 1.5 mm on a side (no floorplan published)

nodes.blurb: Eight minions that share one instruction cache and sit close enough for fast direct links. Esperanto grouped them so because 7 nm wires are slow over longer distances.

facts.text: A neighbourhood is 8 minions sharing a 32 KB L1 instruction cache (128 sets × 4 ways × 64 B), two L0 micro-I-caches (each shared by 4 minions, 16 fully associative 512-bit entries) and a 12-counter PMU.

facts.source: external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.11-13 (§2.1.2); external/et-man/ET Minion Overview.pdf, pdf p.3 (slide 4)

facts.text: Neighbourhood floorplan: two columns of four minions either side of a central 'neighbourhood channel'; left column M2, M0, M4, M6 and right column M3, M1, M5, M7 (north to south); all ports and the high-voltage region are at the north end, where it meets the shire channel.

facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Neigborhood-MAS.pdf pp.7-8 §2.2, Figure 2 'Neighborhood Physical Layout'

facts.text: The eight minions of a neighbourhood sit in its low-voltage (LV) region with their own clock; the neighbourhood says the memory cells of its ICache data RAMs "need to be placed in an HV region", so those RAMs were moved out into the shire channel.

nodes.name: Request path to the banks

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude

nodes.blurb: Where the eight minions' requests queue up: arbiters pick one request at a time, and per-bank queues carry them out of the low-voltage region into the shire's high-voltage channel.

facts.text: Inside the neighbourhood a request passes the minion's Miss/Evict flip-flops, a 2:1 minion arbiter (evicts first), a flop, a two-stage 13:1 round-robin arbiter, a 1-cycle pre-processing stage and then one of five output FIFOs (four banks + UC, 3 entries each, with a 2-entry intermediate FIFO). facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Neigborhood-MAS.pdf, pdf p.16-20 §4.3.1-4.3.5

facts.text: The neighbourhood's request datapath is 256 bits wide (a 512-bit write takes two cycles and is re-joined before the bank FIFO); its response datapath and the ET-Link into each bank are 512 bits; the minion's own fill interface is 256 bits, so a 64 B line reaches the L1 in two beats.

facts.source: external/core-et/docs/CORE-ET-Neigborhood-MAS.pdf, pdf p.18-19 §4.3.4, pdf p.20 §4.4.1, pdf p.45 §7.1 (Figure 16)

nodes.name: Tags, valid and LRU bits

size.label: inferred
size.note: order of magnitude: 2,240 latch bits and 320 flip-flops

nodes.blurb: For each of the 64 lines: which address it holds (a 33-bit tag), its state, whether it is valid, and the order of use that picks the next line to replace.

facts.text: Metadata: 64 entries (16 sets x 4 ways) of tag PA[39:7] (33 bits) + 2-bit line state = 35 bits, held in four latch register files (one per way, 16 entries, read in the same cycle); the 64 valid bits are flip-flops.

facts.source: external/core-et/docs/Minion DCache Description.pdf, pdf p.31 (§3.3, text L1350-1361) and pdf p.57 (§3.12.1, text L2457-2458); external/core-et/rtl/shire/minion/dcache/dcache_metadata_array.v:39-65 (rf_latch_1r_1w per way, valid in RST_EN_FF); external/core-et/rtl/inc/dcache_types.vh:183-187; external/core-et/rtl/libs/rf_latches/rf_latch_1r_1w.v:49-50 ("read latency = 0")

facts.text: Replacement is LRU: 16 bits per set (a 4 x 4 order matrix), in flip-flops, updated in S2 on every cacheable access; hard- and soft-locked ways are excluded when choosing the victim.

facts.source: external/core-et/rtl/inc/dcache_defines.vh:31; external/core-et/rtl/shire/minion/dcache/dcache_lru_array.v (RST_EN_FF per set); external/core-et/rtl/shire/minion/dcache/dcache_top.v:2722-2744, 3150-3159; external/core-et/docs/Minion DCache Description.pdf, pdf p.25 (text L954)

facts.text: Tag first, then data: in S1 the physical tag is compared with all 4 ways (four comparators) and the hit way is encoded; the S2 data read then reads only that way's row, because the way is part of the LRAM row address.

size.label: inferred

nodes.blurb: The 4 KB of data: four latch-RAM blocks side by side, each 128 rows of 64 bits; a row across the four blocks is half a cache line.

facts.text: The data array is not SRAM: it is built from latch RAM, "4 LRAM (Latch-RAM) blocks of 128 rows and 64 bits per row", each block with a single read port and a single write port.

facts.source: external/core-et/docs/Minion DCache Description.pdf, pdf p.29 (§3.2, text L1269-1271) and glossary pdf p.61 ("LRAM Latch Random Access Memory"); external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.9 (§2.1.1.5, text L346)

facts.text: In the RTL each 128 x 64 block is a wrapper of two 128 x 32 one-read-one-write LRAM macros (low and high 32-bit halves) with their own read and write enables: 8 macros (dcache_128x32_1r1w_lram) per minion.

facts.source: external/core-et/rtl/shire/minion/dcache/dcache_data_ram_wrap.v:4-52; external/core-et/rtl/shire/minion/dcache/dcache_data_array.v:119-136; external/core-et/rtl/inc/dcache_defines.vh:50-56

facts.text: LRAM row address = {set[3:0], half-line bit, way[1:0]} = {addr[9:5], way[1:0]}: 7 bits, 128 rows. Address bits [4:3] choose the block (8 bytes each); one row across the 4 blocks is 32 bytes, half a line; a 64-byte line occupies 2 rows, and the 4 ways of a half-line sit in 4 adjacent rows.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/docs/Minion DCache Description.pdf, pdf p.29-30 (§3.2, text L1276-1296, Figure 10); external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.10 (Figure 2-3); external/core-et/rtl/shire/minion/dcache/dcache_data_array.v:46-50

facts.text: Only the blocks a load needs are read: a scalar load enables the one block whose addr[4:3] matches (both of its 32-bit halves); a 32-byte packed-single (PS) vector load enables all four; a misaligned access also reads the next row in the following blocks.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/rtl/shire/minion/dcache/dcache_top.v:2123-2147; external/et-man/ET Preliminary Datasheet Rev 1.0.pdf, pdf p.10 (text L352-361, worked examples)

nodes.name: LRAM block (128 x 64)

size.label: inferred
size.note: 8,192 latch bits (order of magnitude)

nodes.blurb: One block: a write decoder and a clock gate per row on one side, 128 rows of 64 latches, and a read selector that picks one row onto the 64 output wires.

facts.text: The ET latch register-file library ("Latch based Register Files with registered read output") shows the write and read mechanism these arrays use: write data is captured by a low-phase latch clocked by a negative clock gate one phase before the write; the decoded write address enables one per-row clock gate; that row's latches are transparent while its gated clock is high; the read address is registered on the rising edge and the read is a combinational select rf[rd_addr_reg] (no bitline, no sense amplifier in the model).

facts.source: external/core-et/rtl/libs/rf_latches/rf_latch_1r_1w_reg.v:4-52 (timing diagram and notes), 88-96 (write-data latch), 101-136 (per-row clock gates and latches), 139-149 (registered read address, combinational read)

facts.text: The clock gates of the latch arrays are standard cells when the ASIC cell switch is on: HDBULT08_CKGTPLT_V7Y2_2 (rising-edge gate, per row) and HDBULT08_CKGTNLT_V5Y2_2 (falling-edge gate, write-data latch). Other cells named in the RTL come from HDBULT08_* and HDBULT11_* families.
facts.label: spec
facts.source: external/core-et/rtl/libs/rf_latches/et_clk_gate.v:14-18; external/core-et/rtl/libs/rf_latches/et_clk_gate_n.v:14-18; external/core-et/rtl/inc/libs_defines.vh:8-9 (switch off in the open release: "Standard cells not available")

facts.text: A latch-array read is logic: the registered address drives a decoder or a mux tree (128:1 per output bit, e.g. seven 2:1 levels or four 4:1 levels), and only the nodes whose value changes spend energy, so read energy depends on the data.

size.label: inferred
size.note: DRAM cells are tens of nm apart, their capacitors far taller; order of magnitude only

nodes.blurb: A DRAM bit is one transistor and one tiny capacitor: charged is 1, empty is 0. The charge leaks away, so every row is read and rewritten every few tens of milliseconds (refresh).

facts.text: A DRAM bit is one 1T1C cell: an NMOS access transistor whose gate is the wordline and whose drain is the bitline, in series with a storage capacitor; the stored charge is the bit, it leaks away (hence refresh), and reading it is destructive until the sense amplifier restores it.
facts.label: generic
facts.source: GENERIC (textbook DRAM; no ET source describes the die)

facts.text: Each cell shares its charge with its bitline, nudging it slightly above or below the half-voltage; the bitline sense amplifier, a cross-coupled latch of two NMOS and two PMOS, is then fired (NMOS side pulled to ground, PMOS side to the array voltage) and drives the pair to full rail, which also rewrites the cell. The row of latched sense amplifiers is the open page ('row buffer').
facts.label: generic
facts.source: GENERIC (textbook DRAM)

facts.text: Between accesses each bitline pair is held at half the array voltage by a precharge/equalize circuit (typically three NMOS: two tie BL and /BL to the half-voltage, one shorts them together); the equalize signal turns off just before a wordline rises.
facts.label: generic
facts.source: GENERIC (textbook DRAM)

facts.text: All-bank refresh: the die's internal counter supplies the row addresses and each REFab activates and precharges a batch of rows in every bank at once; JEDEC LPDDR4 asks for 8,192 refresh commands per 32 ms retention window at normal temperature, which with 131,072 rows per bank means 16 rows of each bank per REFab.
facts.label: generic
facts.source: GENERIC (JEDEC JESD209-4 tREFW 32 ms, 8,192 REF); rows per bank from dram.org.geometry
